overview: The file combines a 1932 exchange between Harold K. Hochschild of the American Metal Company and State Department Far Eastern Affairs chief Stanley K. Hornbeck concerning Japan’s supplies of the munitions-related nonferrous metals lead, zinc, and copper, with a later American consular report on the rapid expansion of aluminum and hydroelectric-power production in Japanese-ruled Taiwan. The correspondence records trade impressions that Japan continued conspicuous foreign purchases of lead and zinc during the global industrial depression while possessing substantial copper capacity. The 1938 report supplies detailed figures, costs, locations, and construction schedules for aluminum works and four associated power plants in eastern Taiwan; it was recopied and filed for wartime use in 1944.

subfiles.title: Hochschild letter on Japan’s requirements for lead, zinc, and copper
subfiles.about: Hochschild conveys metal-trade assessments of Japan’s production and foreign purchasing of three nonferrous metals important to munitions.
subfiles.summary: Hochschild reports Japan has little domestic lead, buying heavily abroad at lower non-U.S. prices; its lead and zinc purchases stayed active despite the Depression, zinc output is supplemented by imports, and copper capacity likely exceeds domestic need.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment of Hochschild’s metal-market comments
subfiles.about: Hornbeck acknowledges and expresses appreciation for Hochschild’s comments on Japanese lead, copper, and zinc requirements.
subfiles.summary: State thanks Hochschild for his comments on Japan's lead, copper, and zinc needs, recalling their prior dinner meeting.

subfiles.title: Gerald Warner report on aluminum production in Taiwan
subfiles.to: Commercial Office, U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: The report describes current and projected aluminum-smelting capacity in Taiwan and the hydroelectric developments intended to supply a new eastern Taiwan factory.
subfiles.summary: Warner reports Japan Aluminum's Takao plant in Taiwan rising to 8,000-9,000 tons yearly, plus a new Beiron factory targeting 8,000 tons by 1941 powered by four hydroelectric plants, based on a 1938 newspaper account later copied for wartime intelligence use.

interest: Shows Depression-era private intelligence on Japan's lead, zinc, and copper needs, and wartime reuse of a 1938 Taiwan aluminum report.
